principles.line: Design for calibration, not for trust.
principles.detail: The goal is not maximal trust but accurate trust: a user whose confidence matches the system's real reliability. Over-trust (automation misuse) and under-trust (disuse) are both failures. Every pattern in this library is ultimately a calibration device — it moves the user's mental model toward the ground truth of what the system can and cannot do.
refs: Lee & See (2004), Trust in Automation — 'calibrated trust'.
Parasuraman & Riley (1997) — misuse / disuse / abuse.
Mayer, Davis & Schoorman (1995) — Ability / Benevolence / Integrity.

principles.line: Authenticate the verifier to the human before you ask the human for anything.
principles.detail: Wallet identity inverts the classic login: the relying party must prove who it is to the user first, and the interface is the only place that inversion becomes real. Render a compact identity card — legal name, jurisdiction, the authority that vouches for it, the purpose it is registered for — checked against the trust list before the consent screen is ever drawn.
refs: EUDI ARF v2.x — access vs registration certificate.
Trust moment T4 (Counterparty identification), the market's weakest.
Korir, Parkin & Dunphy (2022), SOUPS.

principles.line: Three trust states minimum, and the middle one must be honest.
principles.detail: Binary indicators train users to read the absence of a warning as the presence of safety — the implied truth effect. At least three states are needed, and the middle one must admit uncertainty in plain language: 'the identity of the signer can't be verified.' C2PA's middle-state wording is the exemplar to copy.
refs: C2PA UX Guidance for Implementers v2.2 (CC BY 4.0).
Implied truth effect — an open user-research question flagged in the C2PA spec.

principles.line: Show the proposition, not the data field.
principles.detail: Render the claim being proven and its truth value, not a field with a value: 'Over 18: Yes. Your date of birth is not shared.' The negative clause teaches the privacy property while exercising it. Presenting the credential as an indivisible object throws away the cryptographic advantage and reproduces the all-or-nothing plastic card.
refs: eIDAS 2.0 (Reg. (EU) 2024/1183) Art. 5a — selective disclosure.
Use case UC-01: age assurance without DoB — the best-solved interaction in existence.

principles.line: Never render a hash where a sentence belongs.
principles.detail: Blind signing is the canonical trust-UX failure: never ask a person to sign or approve what they cannot read. Render the effect of an action in human language; keep 'show raw' as an expert affordance, never the default. The EIP-712 / ERC-7730 / ERC-8213 stack exists precisely to make this possible.
refs: EIP-712 (typed data); ERC-7730 (display metadata); ERC-8213 (wallet display).
Anti-pattern AP-04: hash as description.

principles.line: Simulate the outcome. Show what will be true afterward.
principles.detail: Shift the screen from 'do you authorize this instruction?' to 'here is what will be true afterward.' Simulating balance and permission deltas before commit turns a parsing task into a comparison task, which humans do far better. This crypto-wallet reframing is the single largest unexploited pattern transfer into identity disclosure.
refs: Open question: does transaction simulation transfer to identity disclosure? (untested).
Trust moment T5 (Request comprehension).

principles.line: Label computed facts differently from asserted claims.
principles.detail: Distinguish assertions the system produced under its own control (trusted timestamps, device-signed GPS) from assertions gathered from elsewhere (imported EXIF, typed captions). Any interface that mixes measured, derived and declared inputs into one visual treatment is lying by typography. This transfers directly to AI trust scoring.
refs: C2PA: 'recorded by the capture device' vs 'entered by the creator'.
Directly applicable to Validant's AI trust-score surface.

principles.line: Spend friction on irreversibility, and nowhere else.
principles.detail: Confirmation friction is a finite budget, not a free safety measure. Assign each action an irreversibility cost and spend friction against it: reversible low-stakes actions get none; irreversible ones get typed confirmation, re-auth, or a delay. Warnings are a scarce resource — a target warning rate should be treated like a crash rate.
refs: Alert-fatigue / habituation literature.
Anti-pattern AP-05: warning inflation.

principles.line: Every disclosure leaves a receipt the person owns.
principles.detail: Every disclosure event should produce a durable, human-readable, exportable record: timestamp, counterparty, exact attributes released, legal basis, retention. It is the only thing that makes a subject-access request tractable, the only evidence in a dispute, and the only way a person can learn their own disclosure behaviour. Granting and withdrawing must cost the same effort.
refs: Use case UC-10: disclosure history — the biggest gap vs regulatory promise.
DSA Art. 25; EDPB Guidelines 03/2022; CPPA v. American Honda (2025).

principles.line: Say what the system does not prove.
principles.detail: Trust systems accumulate over-attribution in the interface, so the interface is where it must be corrected — in one plain sentence, at the summary level, not buried in an FAQ. Provenance is not veracity; a verified issuer is not a good actor; a trust score is not a guarantee. C2PA does not detect deepfakes or establish truth, and the UI must say so.
refs: C2PA scope disclaimers (provenance ≠ veracity).
Anti-pattern AP-11: sovereignty without affordances.
Finding: the implied truth effect.

layers.name: Agency
layers.responsibility: The moment of decision: comprehension, consent, revocation.

layers.name: Engineering
layers.responsibility: Rendering cryptographic fact into a human statement.

layers.name: Governance
layers.responsibility: Making registry, certification, and scope legible. The waterline is where most trust UX fails.
layers.patterns: Trust marks, purpose binding, three-state display

layers.name: Institutional
layers.responsibility: Priming, mental models, recourse, cultural legitimacy.

iceberg_elements.name: Reciprocity
iceberg_elements.def: Fair, transparent value exchange: rewarding good actions and easing user concern through fairness. The single strongest cue effect on trusting beliefs.

iceberg_elements.name: Brand
iceberg_elements.def: Intangible identity, reputation and consistency. Investing in a brand signals trustworthiness as capital put at risk: a costly, hard-to-fake signal.

iceberg_elements.name: Technical Trust Infrastructure
iceberg_elements.def: The identity, privacy, security and compliance machinery. The interface between the visible cues and the hidden foundations of trust.

iceberg_elements.name: Social Trust Mechanisms
iceberg_elements.def: Community-driven trust: reputation systems, endorsements, moderation and social proof.

iceberg_elements.name: Governance, Resilience & Assurance
iceberg_elements.def: How the organisation keeps trust up over time: adaptive governance, operational resilience, and continuous assurance through audits, monitoring and certifications.

iceberg_elements.name: Contextual Moderation Layer
iceberg_elements.def: The waterline itself. Perceived risk and context (magnitude, culture, domain, user segment) decide which cues are visible and how high a belief must clear before it becomes action.

iceberg_elements.name: Institution-based trust
iceberg_elements.def: Trust in the surrounding system or structure even without prior interaction: structural assurance and situational normality.

iceberg_elements.name: Trusting Beliefs
iceberg_elements.def: The trustor's assessment of the other party, held on two lenses that context switches between: reasoned cognition and felt affect.

iceberg_elements.name: Cognitive beliefs
iceberg_elements.def: Reasoned judgement: competence, benevolence, integrity and predictability for a person; functionality, reliability and helpfulness for a system.

iceberg_elements.name: Affective beliefs
iceberg_elements.def: Emotional trust grounded in empathy, attachment and the felt quality of the relationship.

iceberg_elements.name: Disposition to Trust
iceberg_elements.def: The individual's baseline propensity to trust, shaped by personality and past experience: the same cue lands differently on different people.

iceberg_elements.name: Trusting Intentions & Behaviors
iceberg_elements.def: The willingness to act on trust (buy, share data, delegate) and the act itself: the behavioural outcome every other layer feeds into.

iceberg_elements.name: Trust Formation
iceberg_elements.def: How trust is first built: calculus-based (cost versus benefit), then knowledge-based (from repeated interaction), then identification-based (shared values).

iceberg_elements.name: Trust Calibration
iceberg_elements.def: Keeping perceived trust aligned with actual trustworthiness over time: are the cues relevant, available, detected and used correctly? Where automation bias and algorithm aversion live.

iceberg_elements.name: Trust Repair
iceberg_elements.def: How trust recovers after a violation: competence failures need an apology and a fix; integrity failures need denial plus evidence of principle. The wrong move makes it terminal.

calibration_postures.label: Increase
calibration_postures.def: Meaningful new evidence supports competence, integrity, provenance or control.

calibration_postures.label: Hold
calibration_postures.def: The interaction is routine; no new evidence justifies broader confidence.

calibration_postures.label: Decrease
calibration_postures.def: A mismatch, unexplained change, excessive request or poor outcome appears.

calibration_postures.label: Suspend
calibration_postures.def: Uncertainty is unresolved and the possible consequence exceeds an acceptable threshold.

T1.note: Hold until the inviter, destination, purpose and initial access are corroborated; suspend if it asks for credentials, payment or recovery codes.

T3.note: Increase gradually as storage, authentication, backup, recovery and device revocation are demonstrated; suspend high-value use until recovery is configured.

T10.note: Hold until relationship evidence is inspected; increase only after independent verification, a trusted shared context or cryptographic continuity.

T2.note: Increase after the system confirms which evidence succeeded and what assurance level was established; suspend the enrolment, not the person, when evidence is inconclusive.

T11.note: Increase only for the specific claim and issuer relationship, never the whole profile; suspend publication when a claim is disputed.

T4.note: Hold until the counterparty's domain, identity, purpose and request are bound together; increase only for the specific transaction, never the whole service.

T5.note: Hold during explanation; increase only when the explanation is accurate and the user can actually predict the consequences.

T12.note: Hold while choosing the persona; increase only when the user sees the exact attributes and audience; suspend when the presented identity is undeterminable.

T6.note: Consent itself must not increase trust. Hold unless the request is proportionate and understandable; decrease when refusal is punitive or scopes are bundled.

T7.note: Increase only for the exact reviewed transaction, not globally for the service; decrease if details change between review and confirmation.

T13.note: Conditional hold: increase only through observed, bounded, successful performance; suspend instantly on prompt injection, scope ambiguity or unexpected external action.

T8.note: Maintain or decrease based on freshness, expiry and unexplained activity; suspend affected items while investigating.

T9.note: Suspend affected relationships, credentials, permissions or agents immediately on credible risk; rebuild trust incrementally from verified evidence.

moments.name: Invitation & Onboarding
moments.q: Who invited me, what am I joining, and does accepting connect me to them?
moments.fail: Category confusion / wrong mental model; blind acceptance of an unverified invite; treating a relationship-forming act as a bare account signup.
moments.trustTask: Discovery/Connection/Auth: accept an invitation, which itself forms the person's first trust relationship
moments.def: The front door. A newcomer arrives BY INVITATION from a person or org already in the network; accepting is not a generic signup but the creation of their first trust relationship. This grounds the one moment the white paper leaves essentially UNGROUNDED (Orientation) in the paper's actual entry event, while preserving Orientation's 'what is this / who stands behind it' mental-model concern. Carries a second facet for non-invitation self-serve/discovery entry so it does not misrepresent those flows.

moments.name: Custody & Recovery Setup
moments.q: Where does my secret live, who can reach it, and how do I get back in if I lose my device?
moments.fail: Seed-phrase misunderstanding, lock-out anxiety, no guardians named so recovery is bolted on too late.
moments.trustTask: Wallets & Credentials: key custody + Recover keys (setup, guardians from day one)
moments.def: Where the secret lives, who can reach it, and how the person gets back in after loss, configured UP FRONT. Guardians nominated from day one (Evolution's 'recovery designed up front'); custody explained via progressive disclosure without ever surfacing a raw seed phrase or key. Owns the proactive/setup half of the paper's recovery-vs-revocation separation.

moments.name: Relationship Formation & Recognition
moments.q: Am I really connecting with the person I think, and how will each of us recognize and name this relationship later?
moments.fail: Meaningless DIDs no one can recognize; one-sided/asymmetric connection; correlation leakage during pairing; connecting with an impostor.
moments.trustTask: Discovery/Connection/Auth: form a NEW RELATIONSHIP; exchange business cards / r-cards
moments.def: Establishing a peer-to-peer connection: the pairwise-DID private-channel handshake, the BIDIRECTIONAL VRC pair that constitutes the relationship, PLUS the r-card that turns opaque DIDs into a human-recognizable business card so both sides recognize the tie. Directly fixes the incumbent 9's unidirectional holder to verifier bias and is where the person's trust graph literally begins.

moments.name: Enrollment / Issuance
moments.q: How did this credential get here, is the issuer real, and is it truly bound to me?
moments.fail: Weak holder-binding perception; unverified issuer accepted; the person cannot tell what the credential asserts.
moments.def: The person as HOLDER receives a foundational or functional credential from a verified issuer: the ENROLLMENT phase. Covers the Personhood Credential anchor and delegated credentials. Stays about credentials you RECEIVE; issuing to peers lives in moment 5.

moments.name: Peer Issuance & Vouching
moments.q: How do I vouch for or attest something about someone, and what am I putting my name to?
moments.fail: Holder-only bias leaves the person with no issuing surface; unconsidered over-vouching; not grasping what the attestation commits the issuer to.
moments.trustTask: Wallets & Credentials: ISSUE a peer-to-peer credential (attribute/attestation, distinct from the relationship VRC)
moments.def: The person acting as ISSUER, exercising Representation's 'symmetry of roles' (one coherent mental model whether you are holder, verifier, or issuer). Distinct from moment 3: this is issuing a SUBSTANTIVE functional/attribute attestation ABOUT a peer (e.g. vouching for a skill or role), an asymmetric act, NOT re-issuing the relationship VRC that moment 3 already produced. This is the surface the unidirectional 9 moments entirely omit ('ANYONE can be an issuer, holder, or verifier').

moments.name: Counterparty Identification & Verification
moments.q: Who is the other party right now, are they who they claim, what is their reputation, and if I am being redirected, is the destination legitimate?
moments.fail: Phishing / fake verifier; spoofed or deepfake counterparty; blind redirect to a malicious target; identity confirmed but reputation/authorization ignored.
moments.trustTask: Discovery/Connection/Auth + Verify a counterparty: identification, authorization & reputation; session authentication / login replacement
moments.def: The live 'who is on the other side' screen, made ROLE-SYMMETRIC. As the party being asked, the person establishes who is asking (verified verifier / verified counterparty / unverified-proceed-with-caution, the Formation provenance affordance); as the party doing the asking, the same ceremony serves the person AS VERIFIER (the paper's canonical 'Verify a counterparty' task). Implements the paper's IDENTIFICATION then AUTHORIZATION pairing plus a REPUTATION signal. Also the trust question at any app-to-app redirect. Flagged high-criticality / low-maturity: a gallery priority.

moments.name: Request Comprehension
moments.q: What exactly are they asking for, and why do they need it?
moments.fail: Blind signing; over-disclosure by default; opaque or jargon-laden requests.
moments.trustTask: USAGE authorization : comprehending the ask for a present-a-credential ceremony
moments.def: Making the ask legible: exactly what is requested and why, in plain language, before any signature. The transparency dilemma (enough information, no more) and the anti-blind-signing surface. Kept SEPARATE from the disclosure decision because comprehension failure (blind signing) and decision failure (over-disclosure) are distinct, and comprehension maturity is independently flagged weak: a gallery priority.

moments.name: Persona Selection
moments.q: Which version of me should this party see, and can they link it to my other activity?
moments.fail: Unwanted correlation across contexts; presenting the wrong persona; no unlinkability control.
moments.trustTask: Cross-task persona management : select which persona DID to present + correlation control
moments.def: Choosing which persona DID (public / community / private) to present for THIS context, with correlation/unlinkability control. Kept separate from the disclosure decision because the paper calls it broader than field-level disclosure: persona is WHICH SELF appears; disclosure is WHICH CLAIMS. This moment is the live per-request choice; the standing persona-portfolio / cross-context correlation overview lives in Retrospection & Portfolio (moment 12).

moments.name: Consent & Disclosure Decision
moments.q: What do I release, what do I hold back, and can I decline or share less just as easily as I can agree?
moments.fail: Consent theatre; all-or-nothing disclosure; ZKP mechanics leaking into the UI; a decline path harder or longer than accept (dark pattern).
moments.trustTask: Wallets & Credentials: PRESENT a credential via selective disclosure / ZKP
moments.def: The consent HERO moment. Deciding which claims to release and which to hold back, often via selective disclosure / ZKP (release the minimum, e.g. 'is a unique person', without revealing underlying data; never surface DIDs/keys/ZKP mechanics). Absorbs REFUSAL as its integral decline branch: continuing and declining given equal visual prominence and equal path length, and withdrawing made exactly as easy as giving. Refusal is not a later step, it is the 'no' branch of this same decision, enforced here as a required Control quality.

moments.name: Execution & Confirmation
moments.q: Did it work, was I told before being sent elsewhere, and what exactly did I just do?
moments.fail: Silent success; no proof/receipt; unexplained redirect; the user cannot tell what action was committed.
moments.trustTask: USAGE flow end; carries Payments & value, Secure messaging/file/signing, and Multi-party cross-domain workflows via functional tag
moments.def: The end of the USAGE flow: the action completes and the person gets a receipt / durable proof of exactly what they did and with whom, with offline+online parity. Absorbs any app-to-app HANDOFF/redirect as an Interaction quality (announced before it happens, no more steps than opening the app directly). This is the moment that spans the paper's non-presentation task families (payments, signing, multi-party) via its functional tag.

moments.name: Agent Delegation & Standing Access
moments.q: What is acting on my behalf while I am not watching, for whom does it act, and how do I keep it accountable over time?
moments.fail: Runaway standing permissions; unclear whom the agent serves; no periodic re-confirmation; no human-in-the-loop on consequential actions.
moments.trustTask: Approve an agent action / authenticated delegation & oversight (Part Eight)
moments.def: Authorizing and supervising long-lived access, above all a personal AI agent: authenticated delegation ('who does the agent actually work for?'), scope, human-in-the-loop on sensitive actions, and PERIODIC re-confirmation of standing access that STOPS accessing data if the user does not respond (the maintenance rule). Carries Part Eight's agent tests (Recovery, Fiduciary duty). A note/secondary tag preserves standing-access review for ordinary NON-agent app permissions so they are not orphaned.

moments.name: Retrospection & Portfolio
moments.q: What do I hold, what have I shared and with whom, and can I calmly pull any of it back?
moments.fail: No audit trail; history illegible; asymmetric or absent revocation (easy to grant, hard to undo); persona correlation invisible.
moments.trustTask: Cross-task overview; REVOKE/replace routinely; standing persona-portfolio management
moments.def: The persistent-overview layer: relationships as r-cards, credentials held, personas and their cross-context correlation exposure, active agent grants, and a log of what was shared with whom, all in human terms (circles, reputation, badges, history), never graphs. Routine, non-crisis REVOCATION of a grant/credential/relationship lives here, made symmetric to how it was granted. Flagged weak: a gallery priority.

moments.name: Incident, Recovery & Revocation
moments.q: Something is wrong, or I need to pull something back in a hurry, what are my options?
moments.fail: Dead-end warnings, no recourse; recovery and revocation conflated into one confusing flow; guardians unreachable.
moments.trustTask: Recover keys (guardians) + REVOKE/replace (compromise); two distinct ceremonies
moments.def: The reactive recourse layer. When something is wrong (loss, phishing, compromise, dispute) the person has real options and is never sent to a dead-end warning. It routes to and clearly DISTINGUISHES two flows the paper treats as separate: RECOVERY (regaining access to a lost key/credential via the guardians configured in moment 2) and REVOCATION (compromise-driven withdrawal of a credential or relationship). A mandatory recovery-vs-revocation facet tag forces every screen to declare which flow it shows, so the two are never conflated (the fix for T8's asymmetric-revocation failure).

ux_domains.name: Formation
ux_domains.def: How trust gets created: deciding whom to trust and perceiving the signal.

ux_domains.name: Interaction
ux_domains.def: How trust is exercised in the live moment of a task: the ceremony itself.

ux_domains.name: Control
ux_domains.def: How in-command the user feels: consent, scope, revocation, audit.

ux_domains.name: Explainability
ux_domains.def: How much information is enough: the transparency dilemma.

ux_domains.name: Representation
ux_domains.def: How trust is shown and mentally modeled: circles, family, reputation, badges, history, r-cards, not graphs.

ux_domains.name: Evolution
ux_domains.def: How trust changes over time: grows, decays, is revoked, is recovered.

phases.name: Onboarding & Formation
phases.note: Getting in and forming the first relationships

phases.name: Credentials & Issuance
phases.note: Receiving credentials, and issuing to peers

phases.name: The Live Ceremony
phases.note: The recurring proof, once per transaction

journey.what: Maya taps an invite from a friend already in the network. The screen names the inviter, explains what the First Person Network is, and makes clear that accepting is not a bare signup but the start of her first trust relationship. DID mechanics stay hidden.

Before holding anything valuable, her wallet is created; she learns in plain language where her key lives (never shown as a raw seed phrase) and nominates two guardians, so recovery exists before she ever needs it.

Accepting runs the pairwise-DID handshake with the inviter over a private channel; both receive a human-readable r-card and exchange the bidirectional VRC pair, exactly like adding a contact on Signal.
Maya provides evidence and receives her Personhood Credential from a verified issuer (evidence, checks, PHC issued); holder-binding is made perceptible so she trusts it is genuinely hers.
Acting now as an issuer, Maya vouches for a classmate by issuing a skill attestation; the UI shows precisely what she is attesting and that she, not just the holder, is on record for it.

A rental platform asks her to prove she is a real, unique person. Before revealing anything she confirms WHO is asking (verified verifier vs proceed-with-caution) and sees its reputation; the browser-to-wallet redirect is announced and frictionless.
She reads exactly what is requested and why, in plain language, with nothing hidden behind a blind signature.
She chooses which persona to present, her public/rental persona rather than her private one, and confirms it will not correlate with her other selves.
The hero screen: via ZKP she discloses only 'unique person + over 18' without revealing her name or birth date. The decline / share-less path is exactly as prominent and as short as proceeding.
She confirms; the proof is sent, the platform shows clear success, and she keeps a receipt of exactly what she shared and with whom, working the same online or offline.

She authorizes a personal AI agent to renew such proofs on her behalf; she sets scope, sees the agent works for HER, keeps human-in-the-loop on sensitive steps, and the system re-confirms this standing access periodically and pauses if she does not respond.

A dashboard shows her relationships as r-cards, credentials, personas and their correlation exposure, and a log of everything shared, in human terms; she calmly revokes one routine grant she no longer needs.

She loses her phone. She hits no dead-end: she recovers her keys via her guardians (recovery) and, separately, revokes a VRC she had issued to someone she no longer trusts (revocation), two clearly labeled and distinct flows.

best_practices.title: Verifier identity card before the ask
best_practices.what: Before showing any data request, render a compact identity card for the requesting party: legal name, jurisdiction, the authority that vouches for it, and the credential it operates under, checked against the trust list before the consent screen is drawn.
best_practices.why: It inverts the phishing economics: in wallet identity the relying party must authenticate to the user first, and the UI is the only place that inversion becomes real.
best_practices.useCase: Scan a QR at a car-rental desk: 'Europcar International SA, registered in France, access certificate issued by ANTS, registered to request: driving-licence category, name, age over 21.'

best_practices.title: Three-state trust display, never binary
best_practices.what: Trust status needs at least three states, and the middle one must be honest: Verified, Unknown/unverifiable, Flagged/invalid. C2PA's middle-state language is exemplary: 'the identity of the signer can't be verified.'
best_practices.why: Binary indicators train users to read absence of warning as presence of safety (the implied truth effect).
best_practices.useCase: A Content Credentials L1 badge expands to 'Signed by [org], but we could not confirm this signer against a recognized authority.'

best_practices.title: Purpose binding, mismatch as a first-class warning
best_practices.what: The EUDI architecture separates the access certificate (who you are) from the registration certificate (what you're registered to ask for). When the declared scope and the actual request diverge, that divergence is the highest-value fact on screen.
best_practices.why: It converts a governance-registry artifact into an actionable consumer protection at the exact moment of vulnerability.
best_practices.useCase: 'Registered to request: age over 18. Currently asking for: full name, date of birth, home address. Three attributes fall outside its registered purpose.' With a one-tap report path.

best_practices.title: Name the trust source, not just the verdict
best_practices.what: Every trust assertion should be traceable in one tap to who says so. 'Verified issuer' expands to 'Listed on the Swiss federal Base Registry since 2025-03-14.'
best_practices.why: The difference between a trust mark and a trust claim with provenance; it also degrades gracefully as timestamps age.
best_practices.useCase: Tap 'Trusted' to reveal the trust list, its publisher, and last-update timestamp.

best_practices.title: Attribute-level disclosure, minimum-necessary defaults
best_practices.what: The request screen lists individual claims, not a credential. Each claim is a row; optional claims are toggles default-off; required claims are marked with the reason inline.
best_practices.why: Presenting the credential as an indivisible object reproduces the all-or-nothing plastic card and throws away the cryptographic advantage.
best_practices.useCase: Bar entry reads only 'Age over 18 (required)'. Non-requested attributes do not appear at all.

best_practices.title: Predicate proofs rendered as human statements
best_practices.what: Show the proposition being proven and its truth value, not a field with a value. Best form: 'Over 18: Yes. Your date of birth is not shared.'
best_practices.why: Only that form teaches the privacy property while exercising it; the negative clause does as much work as the positive.
best_practices.useCase: Age-gated retail, EUDI age attestation, online age assurance under UK OSA / EU DSA.

best_practices.title: Clear signing: render effect, never the digest
best_practices.what: Blind signing is the canonical trust-UX failure. EIP-712 (typed data), ERC-7730 (display metadata), ERC-8213 (what the wallet must display) form the remediation stack. Never present a hash as a description; a 'show raw' affordance for experts, never the default.
best_practices.why: Never ask a person to sign what they cannot read.
best_practices.useCase: A Permit2 approval renders as 'You are allowing [contract] to spend up to 50 USDC until 14 August 2026.' Unlimited allowance gets a distinct, louder treatment.

best_practices.title: Outcome simulation and before/after preview
best_practices.what: Simulate the transaction and show the projected balance and permission deltas before commit. It reframes the screen from 'do you authorize this instruction' to 'here is what will be true afterward.'
best_practices.why: Shifts the cognitive task from parsing to comparing, which humans do vastly better. The largest single unexploited pattern transfer between crypto and identity wallets.
best_practices.useCase: Identity equivalent: 'After this, [org] will know your surname, your city, and that you hold a valid Swiss residence permit. They will not learn your date of birth or address.'

best_practices.title: Fixed-level progressive disclosure (L1 to L4)
best_practices.what: C2PA defines four named disclosure levels: L1 Indicator (persistent, scannable mark), L2 Summary (compact card), L3 Detail (full provenance, navigable), L4 Forensic (complete technical detail).
best_practices.why: The naming gives a cross-vendor vocabulary. Most progressive disclosure guidance is a principle; this is a schema, and schemas let ecosystems converge.
best_practices.useCase: Adopt L1-L4 as the disclosure-depth axis for any trust interface, including AI trust scoring.

best_practices.title: Separate computed facts from asserted claims
best_practices.what: Distinguish assertions created by the signer under system control (trusted timestamps, device-signed GPS) from assertions gathered from elsewhere (imported EXIF, typed captions). Label them distinctly; never present as equivalent.
best_practices.why: The single most transferable idea in the corpus: any interface mixing measured, derived and declared inputs into one treatment is lying by typography. Applies directly to AI trust scoring.
best_practices.useCase: 'Recorded by the capture device' versus 'Entered by the creator.'

best_practices.title: Friction proportional to irreversibility
best_practices.what: Assign each action an irreversibility cost and spend interaction friction against it: reversible low-stakes get none; irreversible get typed confirmation, biometric re-auth, or a delay.
best_practices.why: Friction spent on reversible actions is friction stolen from irreversible ones. Confirmation dialogs are a finite budget, not a free safety measure.
best_practices.useCase: Irreversible plus a live threat signal: block, with a deliberately hard override.

best_practices.title: Warnings as a scarce resource with a budget
best_practices.what: High-frequency, low-specificity alerts produce habituation and lower trust in the warning system itself. Use simple messages with evidence, deliberate blocking vs non-blocking, polymorphic warnings, required input for the top tier.
best_practices.why: Alert fatigue is real and measured.
best_practices.useCase: Set a target warning rate per active user per month and treat exceeding it as a defect, like a crash rate.

best_practices.title: Named uncertainty, with the stakes attached
best_practices.what: Never present a probabilistic output with the same weight as a fact, nor the same confidence label across different stakes. Three required components: the confidence signal, what drives it, and a different UI state/action at each threshold.
best_practices.why: 75% confidence means something entirely different for a product recommendation than a compliance flag. Below a usable threshold the correct output is a human-review prompt, not a low number.
best_practices.useCase: Directly relevant to an AI trust-score surface.

best_practices.title: Progressive delegation: autonomy earned
best_practices.what: Start an autonomous system with narrow authority and expand it as the user's approval history demonstrates reliability: approve every action, then batch-approve routine categories, then notify-only, with demotion available at any time.
best_practices.why: The trust-calibration curve made operational; the delegation history is itself the audit trail. Final-step human approval alone is a documented, exploited bypass, so expose the bounds (limits, allowlists, scopes) as first-class.
best_practices.useCase: Agentic commerce and delegated wallet authority; mandate-based flows with signed instructions and daily spend limits.

best_practices.title: Skeuomorphic anchoring for novel credentials
best_practices.what: swiyu renders the credential with a monospace typeface evoking the Swiss passport and holographic accent colours, while the wallet shell uses sans-serif. The credential looks like a document; the container looks like an app.
best_practices.why: Imports thirty years of institutional trust in the physical artifact, and separates the thing-being-trusted from the thing-doing-the-holding.
best_practices.useCase: Caution: security-document visual language on a self-asserted credential would be trust theatre of the worst kind.

best_practices.title: The disclosure receipt
best_practices.what: Every disclosure event produces a durable, human-readable, exportable record: timestamp, counterparty identity, exact attributes released, legal basis, retention claimed, transcript reference. Presented as a searchable activity log.
best_practices.why: The highest-leverage under-built pattern: the only thing that makes a subject-access request tractable, the only evidence in a dispute, and the only way a person can learn their own disclosure behaviour.
best_practices.useCase: Almost no shipping wallet does this well.

best_practices.title: Symmetric effort for grant and withdrawal
best_practices.what: If granting takes one tap, withdrawing takes one tap. Asymmetric consent is now legal exposure under EDPB dark-pattern categories, DSA Art. 25, and FTC Section 5.
best_practices.why: The 2025 CPPA action against American Honda (extensive form to opt out) is the reference case.
best_practices.useCase: Design test: count the taps, screens, and fields in each direction. If unequal, the design is obstructing.

best_practices.title: Recovery designed before onboarding
best_practices.what: Present the recovery model before key generation. State the three non-obvious rules at generation (order matters; nobody legitimate asks for it; there is no reset). Offer social/threshold recovery as a first-class named quorum. Rehearse a recovery drill in onboarding.
best_practices.why: The most consistent finding in the custody literature: users misunderstand what the seed phrase is and what happens on device loss (CHI 2025, n=643; Ontario n=47).
best_practices.useCase: '3 of 5 trusted contacts', not an advanced setting.

best_practices.title: Every warning carries a recourse path
best_practices.what: Every risk state needs at least three exits: proceed with informed acceptance, abandon safely, and dispute. MetaMask's false-positive reporting flow is the reference implementation.
best_practices.why: A warning that dead-ends teaches users that warnings are noise. The dispute path makes the trust system accountable, not merely authoritative.
best_practices.useCase: A form of the redress that regulation (AI Act) increasingly presumes exists.

best_practices.title: State what the system does not prove
best_practices.what: Trust systems accumulate over-attribution. C2PA does not detect deepfakes, does not detect AI generation absent disclosure, and does not establish truth. Provenance is not veracity.
best_practices.why: The interface is where over-attribution forms, so the interface is where it must be corrected, at L2, in one plain sentence, not in the FAQ.
best_practices.useCase: A verified issuer is not a good actor; a trust score is not a guarantee.

exemplars.what: Separates invitation review from final confirmation and asks you to choose the workspace the external relationship will live in, before you accept.
Quarantines unknown contacts: you inspect the context and choose Accept, Delete, Block or Report before the sender gains an ordinary conversation state.
An explicit invitation lifecycle — expiry, retry, edit and cancel — visible to administrators, so joining is never an open-ended auto-join.
Folds creation, authentication, storage and sync into the OS credential experience and shows where the passkey actually lives.
Communicates plainly that recovery responsibility has transferred to the user and the key must be stored separately — no silent provider reset.
Unusually explicit boundary-setting: Signal cannot reset the PIN, it is not a backup, and registration lock may impose a waiting period.
QR or numeric comparison over a separate channel with a local verified state, stating plainly that it authenticates the encrypted relationship, not real-world identity.
Reduces transcription burden by comparing a short sequence of human-recognisable symbols across devices instead of a long key.
Plain-language preparation, alternative routes, app-based document-chip reading, facial matching and in-person options as first-class paths.
Stepwise document capture and video-selfie guidance ending on a screen that shows exactly what identity information will be shared with the relying organisation.
Recipient-controlled social attestation: recommendations require acceptance, and endorsements can be hidden, disabled or removed by the subject.
Separates issuance from earner acceptance and subsequent public sharing, so a claim is not attached to you until you accept it.
Unusually complete counterparty disclosure: the requester, the exact data fields, the stated purpose, and whether the site intends to store them.
Standardises application identity, policy links and requested authorization scopes, decomposed into named resource/action permissions.
Visually distinguishes requested repository reach from account permissions and advises the user to verify the app's owner.
A layered, comparative label that improved users' ability to answer privacy questions and reduced task time in a 200-participant study.

exemplars.product: Sign in with Apple / Hide My Email
exemplars.what: Offers a choice between sharing a verified email and using a provider-generated relay address — the user picks which self to present.
Contact initiation without treating a username as a permanent public identity, with explicit control over phone-number visibility and discoverability.
A system-controlled, one-time permission that separates tracking authorization from the application's own persuasive interface.
Permission categories are managed independently and can be changed after the initial request, not bundled into one all-or-nothing grant.
Renders human-readable recipient, amount, function and contract details on the hardware signer rather than asking the user to approve opaque data.
Presents recipient, payment method, fees and arrival estimate in a review step before an explicit 'Continue and send' commitment.
Pauses for explicit confirmation before certain consequential actions and uses active supervision (watch mode) in sensitive logged-in contexts.
Read-only commands run by default; edits and system-changing commands require approval, with per-action or broader automatic modes.
Open an ID to see where it was presented, inspect issuer details, and delete recent presentation activity stored on the device.
Inventories passwords and passkeys, identifies compromised combinations and directs remediation from the same surface.
Presents recent security events and asks the user to classify suspicious activity ('No, it wasn't me') before guiding remediation.
Prioritises immediate revocation of compromised credentials, log inspection and replacement of affected secrets.
A reserved official badge, a distinct non-interactive chat treatment and explicit 'we will never ask' rules, with direct Report and Block guidance.

use_cases.name: Age assurance without date-of-birth disclosure
use_cases.note: Best-solved trust interaction in existence. Canonical teaching example.

use_cases.name: Unknown verifier requests identity attributes
use_cases.note: Highest criticality-to-maturity gap in the identity domain.

use_cases.name: Token approval with unlimited allowance
use_cases.note: Crypto's most mature warning surface. Directly transferable.

use_cases.name: Off-chain signature request (Permit / Permit2)
use_cases.note: The current live attack surface. Wallets still weak here.

use_cases.name: Seed phrase generation and backup
use_cases.note: Best-studied, still unsolved. Rich anti-pattern material.

use_cases.name: Social / threshold recovery quorum setup
use_cases.note: Emerging. Very few good visual models exist.

use_cases.name: Cross-device QR handoff
use_cases.note: Repeatedly identified as a mental-model mismatch and accessibility barrier.

use_cases.name: Credential issuance and holder binding
use_cases.note: Under-designed. Users doubt their own credential's authenticity.

use_cases.name: Credential revocation or suspension notice
use_cases.note: Almost entirely undesigned. Large open opportunity.

use_cases.name: Disclosure history / activity log
use_cases.note: The biggest gap relative to regulatory promise.

use_cases.name: Content provenance inspection (L1 to L4)
use_cases.note: The reference implementation of layered trust disclosure.

use_cases.name: AI-generated content source disclosure
use_cases.note: Implied truth effect is the live design problem.

use_cases.name: AI output with confidence and stakes
use_cases.note: Directly relevant to Validant's score surface.

use_cases.name: Agent delegation scope setup
use_cases.note: The next frontier. Very little prior art.

use_cases.name: Agent action approval in flight
use_cases.note: Human-in-the-loop bypass is a documented exploited failure mode.

use_cases.name: Reporting a false positive or bad actor
use_cases.note: Rarely designed. Cheap to add, disproportionate trust value.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Name the relying party and list exactly what will be shared BEFORE the user authorises, every time.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: When a user initiates presentation of 1 or more credentials (fully or partially), the facilitation mechanism must notify the user of all the following: (1) the personal or organisational information to be presented; and (2) the relying party to whom the personal or organisational information is being presented, where not being presented in-person.
prescriptive_rules.source: Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Rules 2024 (consolidated) · Department of Internal Affairs / Public Service Commission, New Zealand
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Users decide about the counterparty before they decide about the data. A disclosure UI that leads with attributes answers the second question first.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Display the relying party's trading or brand name - the name the user would recognise - not its legal entity name or client ID.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must display the company's trading name/brand name (i.e. the Client Name) to the PSU during the setup and revocation of consent.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Legal entity names are frequently unrecognisable to the people who must judge them. Recognition is the whole function of the disclosure.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Give the user a way to tell your genuine authentication screen from a spoof, such as a personalised element only you could know.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Identifying your firm as genuine - For example have personalised greetings during authentication so that the PSU knows they are authenticating with their own ASPSP and not a fake.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Redirection flows train users to expect a hand-off to an unfamiliar screen, which is exactly the condition phishing exploits.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Warn the user to share only with relying parties they recognise, at the moment of sharing.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: a warning about sharing their information only to relying parties they know
prescriptive_rules.source: Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Rules 2024 (consolidated) · Department of Internal Affairs / Public Service Commission, New Zealand
prescriptive_rules.rationale: A wallet cannot verify that a legitimate-but-unknown verifier is appropriate for this user; only the user can.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Group requested data into named clusters at the top level and let the user drill down to individual fields. Do not present a flat list of raw attribute names.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Both AISPs and ASPSPs must describe the data being shared at a Data Cluster level and allow the PSU to 'drill-down' to see the detail at Permission level
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Progressive disclosure applied to the attribute list itself. A flat list of 14 technical field names is unreadable; four named groups are.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Request only the data the service actually needs, and suppress request categories that are irrelevant to the product.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: The AISP must ensure they have business rules that manage the relationship between data cluster to product type and omit access to data clusters that are irrelevant
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Data minimisation enforced at the request-construction layer rather than left to the user's refusal.

prescriptive_rules.statement: State explicitly whether any third party beyond the immediate recipient will get the data.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must provide PSUs with sufficient information to enable PSUs to make an informed decision, for example, detail the purpose for which the data will be used (including whether any other parties will have access to the information) the period over which it has been requested and when the consent for the account information will expire
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Onward sharing is the disclosure users most consistently fail to anticipate, and it is routinely omitted from consent screens.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Never bundle unrelated permissions into the transaction the user came to complete.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Trust Framework providers must not require the user to provide authorisation, consent or permission for any activity not directly related to completing the accredited digital identity service being undertaken.
prescriptive_rules.source: Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Rules 2024 (consolidated) · Department of Internal Affairs / Public Service Commission, New Zealand
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Bundling converts a specific consent into a general one by exploiting the user's need to finish the task.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Default every optional data setting to the most protective value. If you deviate, you must be able to justify it.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Settings must be 'high privacy' by default (unless you can demonstrate a compelling reason for a different default setting, taking account of the best interests of the child).
prescriptive_rules.source: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services (Children's Code) · Information Commissioner's Office, UK
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Defaults are the single most powerful determinant of outcome because most users never change them.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Do not use nudges, visual weighting or emotive language to steer users toward disclosing more.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Do not use nudge techniques to lead or encourage children to provide unnecessary personal data or weaken or turn off their privacy protections.
prescriptive_rules.source: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services (Children's Code) · Information Commissioner's Office, UK
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Steering is measurable and auditable in a way that 'clarity' is not.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Ask for consent once, at the party that has the context to explain it. Do not re-ask at the credential holder.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: While an ASPSP may provide additional information and clarification throughout the journey, at no stage should the ASPSP seek to reconfirm or check that the PSU wants the TPP to perform the activity they have consented to.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Treats re-confirmation as a DEFECT rather than a safety feature. The party that can explain the consent captures it; the credential holder authenticates identity only.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Give continuing and declining equal visual prominence and equal path length.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must allow the PSU to explicitly reconfirm their consent with equal prominence given to continue or discontinue the service
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Symmetry is a measurable, auditable design commitment. 'Clarity' is not.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Make withdrawing consent exactly as easy as giving it.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: the process for withdrawing consent is as easy for the Subject as providing consent.
prescriptive_rules.source: Pan-Canadian Trust Framework - Notice & Consent, and Digital Wallet Component Overview · DIACC, Canada
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Asymmetry between entry and exit is the defining property of a roach-motel dark pattern.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Cap the exit path at one friction screen, then confirm.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Once the PSU has clicked 'Disconnect', the AISP should only provide one screen prior to cancelling... A confirmation screen should be provided after this
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Converts 'don't obstruct' into a countable limit. One screen is legitimate confirmation; two or more is obstruction.

prescriptive_rules.statement: On revocation, state plainly what happens to data already shared.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: The confirmation screen must confirm what happens to any existing data... AISPs must ensure that they are fair and transparent about how existing data is processed
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Users routinely assume revocation is retroactive deletion. It usually is not, and the gap between assumption and reality is where trust breaks.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Put the consent dashboard no more than two clicks from home.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Dashboards must be easy and intuitive for PSUs to find and use... positioned... no more than two clicks from the AISP's Home Screen
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: A quantified discoverability requirement rather than an aspiration. Directly testable.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Keep a holder-accessible log recording time, what was requested, what was actually presented, and to whom.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: An audit log, accessible by the Holder, must record the time of the transaction, claims requested and presented, verifier details
prescriptive_rules.source: Pan-Canadian Trust Framework - Notice & Consent, and Digital Wallet Component Overview · DIACC, Canada
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Comprehension at the moment of consent is unreliable, so the record after the fact is what makes disclosure verifiable.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Use a small fixed set of status values on the dashboard, not free-form or graded states.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must use just two status flags: 'Active' or 'Reconfirm'
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Categorical and learnable rather than scalar. Two states can be recognised at a glance across dozens of rows.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Use the vocabulary users have actually learned, not your internal terminology.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must carefully consider the naming of their Dashboard... AISPs must use the preferred term 'open banking connections'
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: An ecosystem-wide mandated term beats per-vendor invention, because recognition compounds across services.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Retain cancelled and expired consents in history, with their original parameters.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must make available all the cancelled or expired consent including details of consent parameters under history
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: A log that only shows live grants cannot answer the question users actually ask: what did I once give away?

prescriptive_rules.statement: Authentication via redirect must take no more steps than opening your app directly.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: the redirection must invoke the ASPSP app for authentication purposes only without introducing any additional screens. The ASPSP app based authentication must have no more than the number of steps that the PSU would experience when directly accessing the ASPSP mobile app (biometric, passcode, credentials).
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Converts 'do not add friction' into a testable parity assertion with a concrete baseline.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Tell the user before the hand-off that they are about to be sent elsewhere, and on return that the session has closed.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs should make the PSU aware on the inbound redirection screen that they will be taken to their ASPSP for authentication for account access.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: An unexplained context switch is indistinguishable from a phishing redirect.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Cross-device handoff must not require the user to retype anything.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: PSUs should be able to easily use the QR code presented by the PISP application (e.g. scan the code on their mobile device from the Desktop in this instance) without much friction (e.g manually entering an alphanumeric code).
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Manual code entry is where cross-device flows fail, and it fails hardest for the users with the least tolerance for it.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Tell the user where the point of no return is, before they cross it.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: ASPSPs should inform PSUs about their 'point of no return' for making the payment and that their payment will be made after pressing the Proceed button.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Irreversibility is the property users most need signalled and most often discover afterwards.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Re-confirm long-lived access periodically, and stop accessing data if the user does not respond.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs must alert the PSU when reconfirmation of consent is required... AISPs must not access data if the PSU has not reconfirmed consent
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Consent decays. Silence must default to withdrawal, not continuation.

prescriptive_rules.statement: When re-confirming, state explicitly that nothing else about the arrangement is changing.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: AISPs should make it clear that the PSU is being asked to authenticate to extend the AISP access to their account data and that no other element of the consent... will change
prescriptive_rules.source: UK Open Banking Customer Experience Guidelines (CEG) and CEG Checklist · Open Banking Limited
prescriptive_rules.rationale: A re-consent prompt that looks like a new request invites either blind acceptance or unnecessary churn.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Notify the user of any change to their digital identity, including requests to close it.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: You must tell the user if any changes have been made to their digital identity. You must also tell them if you've had a request to close their digital identity account.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK digital identity and attributes trust framework · Department for Science, Innovation and Technology / OfDIA, UK
prescriptive_rules.rationale: An account-closure request the legitimate user did not make is the clearest possible takeover signal.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Re-ask for agreement when you substantively change how data is handled.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: If you make substantive changes to the way your product or service handles users' data, you must ask the user to renew their agreement.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK digital identity and attributes trust framework · Department for Science, Innovation and Technology / OfDIA, UK
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Consent is to a specific arrangement, not to a relationship.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Overloading: do not bury the protective choice under an avalanche of options.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: users are confronted with an avalanche/large quantity of requests, information, options or possibilities
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Category 1 - Overloading (sub-patterns: Continuous prompting, Privacy Maze, Too many options)
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Volume itself is the manipulation. Every option is individually defensible; the aggregate is not.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Skipping: do not design the journey so the data-protection decision is passed over.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: designing the interface or user journey in a way that the users forget or do not think about all or some of the data protection aspects
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Category 2 - Skipping (sub-patterns: Deceptive snugness, Look over there)
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: Stirring: do not use emotional framing or visual nudges to move the disclosure decision.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: affects the choice users would make by appealing to their emotions or using visual nudges
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Category 3 - Stirring (sub-patterns: Emotional Steering, Hidden in plain sight)
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: Obstructing: do not make the protective action hard or impossible to complete.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: an obstruction or blocking of users in their process of getting informed or managing their data by making the action hard or impossible to achieve
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Category 4 - Obstructing (sub-patterns: Dead end, Longer than necessary, Misleading action)
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: Fickle: do not vary your data-protection interface between contexts.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: the design of the interface is inconsistent and not clear, making it hard for users to navigate the different data protection control tools
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Category 5 - Fickle (sub-patterns: Lacking hierarchy, Decontextualising, Inconsistent interface, Language discontinuity)
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: Left in the dark: do not hide controls or leave the user unsure how data is processed.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: an interface is designed in a way to hide information or data protection control tools or to leave users unsure of how their data is processed
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Category 6 - Left in the dark (sub-patterns: Conflicting information, Ambiguous wording or information)
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: Use one term for one concept across the entire ecosystem, and define any unavoidable jargon in place.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Across the website, the same wording and definition is used for the same data protection
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: Deliver short contextual explanations at the decision point, in addition to - not instead of - the full policy.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: in addition to an exhaustive privacy policy, bring short bits of information at the most appropriate time for the user
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Progressive disclosure applied to legal text.

prescriptive_rules.statement: When you change a privacy notice, keep prior versions accessible and highlight what changed.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: When changes are made to the privacy notice, make previous versions accessible with date of release and highlight changes
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: Best practice - Change spotting and comparison
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board

prescriptive_rules.statement: When offering a choice of identity providers or wallets, make every option visually equal in size and weight.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Do design sign-in options that are uniform in width and height
prescriptive_rules.source: Login.gov developer user-experience guidance · General Services Administration / 18F, USA
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Unequal styling in a provider chooser is a thumb on the scale. Uniformity is auditable.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Do not use an external-link icon on a sign-in control - it reads as leaving for an untrusted site.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Don't use the external-link icon that might suggest a link to another website
prescriptive_rules.source: Login.gov developer user-experience guidance · General Services Administration / 18F, USA
prescriptive_rules.rationale: A genuine trust-signal rule with a stated reason: the icon imports the wrong mental model at the moment of authentication.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Never use an icon alone where a text label carries the meaning.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Don't use an icon instead of a text label
prescriptive_rules.source: Login.gov developer user-experience guidance · General Services Administration / 18F, USA

prescriptive_rules.statement: Do not reveal which credential was wrong.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Provide secure error feedback
prescriptive_rules.source: U.S. Web Design System - authentication page templates · General Services Administration, USA
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Naming the wrong field enables account enumeration. This is a deliberate, documented trade of usability for security - and worth stating as such rather than pretending it is free.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Allow password visibility toggling and permit paste.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Allow users to toggle password visibility
prescriptive_rules.source: U.S. Web Design System - authentication page templates · General Services Administration, USA
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Blocking paste breaks password managers, which pushes users toward weaker, memorable credentials.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Usability-test with a demographically diverse panel, as a condition of accreditation.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: a diverse range of individuals, covering diversity in disability, age, gender and ethnicity
prescriptive_rules.source: Digital ID (Accreditation) Rules 2024 (F2024L01438) and Explanatory Statement · Australian Government
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Makes inclusion a gate rather than an aspiration. Rare: a legally binding requirement to run user research.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Always offer more than one route to prove the same thing.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: You should always make sure users have more than one way to use your product or service.
prescriptive_rules.source: UK digital identity and attributes trust framework · Department for Science, Innovation and Technology / OfDIA, UK
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Single-route verification silently excludes whoever lacks that route.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Tell the user, unmistakably, whenever they are being monitored or tracked.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: If your online service allows a parent or carer to monitor their child's online activity or track their location, provide an obvious sign to the child when they are being monitored.
prescriptive_rules.source: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services (Children's Code) · Information Commissioner's Office, UK
prescriptive_rules.rationale: The archetypal trust-signal rule: covert observation is the failure, and the signal must be present at the time, not disclosed in a policy.

prescriptive_rules.statement: For age thresholds using estimation, apply an explicit safety buffer and publish demographic-split accuracy.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: It is important for facial age estimation algorithms to be independently evaluated
prescriptive_rules.source: Making age checks inclusive; Facial Age Estimation White Paper · Yoti
prescriptive_rules.rationale: A buffer (e.g. requiring an estimated 25+ to pass an 18+ check) trades false-accept risk against false-reject exclusion, and that trade should be stated numerically rather than hidden.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Treat every prompt as spending a finite attention budget, and be able to state what each one buys.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: users are confronted with an avalanche/large quantity of requests
prescriptive_rules.source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on Deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces · European Data Protection Board
prescriptive_rules.rationale: The regulator and the economics agree: repeated prompting is both a compliance failure and an attention-budget failure.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Cut screens that do not carry a decision, and rewrite the rest in plain language - then measure completion.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: use more plain language to describe the interactions required for verification
prescriptive_rules.source: Security is Everyone's Responsibility: Delivering Secure, Usable Login for Government · Digital.gov / GSA, USA
prescriptive_rules.rationale: The clearest published evidence that identity-proofing UX changes move completion rates.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Treat transparency as making available WHEN AI is used, HOW it works, and WHAT it can and cannot do, tailored to who is asking.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: In its broadest meaning, transparency refers to the availability of information about AI systems, such as when they are being used, how they work, and their capabilities and limitations.
prescriptive_rules.ruleRef: What is transparency, why does it matter?
prescriptive_rules.source: Enhancing Trust in AI Through Increased Transparency · Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2026)
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Different audiences need different transparency: a consumer needs to know they are dealing with AI; a regulator needs design and performance data. One disclosure does not serve all.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Disclose when a person is interacting with an AI system rather than a human, wherever they could reasonably be unaware.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: An individual using a chatbot to generate audiovisual content would almost certainly know that they are interacting with an AI system, whereas a consumer engaging with a customer service chatbot that is not identified as such may be unaware that they are interacting with a machine, rather than a human.
prescriptive_rules.source: Enhancing Trust in AI Through Increased Transparency · Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2026)
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Whether disclosure matters is contextual: redundant when the AI is obvious, load-bearing when the system could be mistaken for a person. Over-disclosing everywhere causes its own fatigue.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Publish a system's capabilities, limitations and appropriate uses (model / system cards) so users can judge fitness and organisations can procure responsibly.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Model cards typically describe a model's capabilities, limitations, and appropriate uses, helping prospective users determine whether it is suited to a task, while system cards describe how a deployed system behaves in practice, including the safeguards built around it.
prescriptive_rules.source: Enhancing Trust in AI Through Increased Transparency · Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2026)
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Deployed outside its intended context and without stated limits, a capable model is routinely trusted where it should not be. The interface must carry what the system does NOT do.

prescriptive_rules.statement: For AI-generated content, mark origin durably and carry provenance in metadata, not on a visible label alone.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Many generative AI developers now mark AI-generated content with hidden watermarks and include provenance information in metadata.
prescriptive_rules.source: Enhancing Trust in AI Through Increased Transparency · Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2026)
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Watermarks are brittle and easy to strip, so durable provenance (C2PA-style) must back the visible cue. Labelling frequent, expected AI edits also produces banner blindness.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Record AI incidents and report serious ones, so causes and trends are understood in time to mitigate proactively rather than reactively.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: As AI is increasingly integrated into products, services, and processes, a better and more timely understanding of AI incidents along with their causes and trends becomes increasingly important.
prescriptive_rules.source: Enhancing Trust in AI Through Increased Transparency · Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2026)
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Incident visibility today leans on voluntary public reports, leaving governments, researchers and the public with an incomplete picture of how often AI failures occur and how well they are handled.

prescriptive_rules.statement: Make an agent's granted permissions, when it is acting on the user's behalf, and how to reverse its actions visible and legible.
prescriptive_rules.verbatim: Users may not always know what permissions have been granted to the agent, when an AI system is acting on their behalf, whether a human remains in control, or how to challenge or reverse an action that an agent has taken.
prescriptive_rules.source: Enhancing Trust in AI Through Increased Transparency · Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2026)
prescriptive_rules.rationale: Autonomy without a visible permission scope, a clear 'who is acting now' signal, and a reversal path removes the very oversight that makes delegation safe.

rule_strengths.label: Research (qualitative)
rule_strengths.def: Backed by published qualitative research; directional

findings.title: C2PA forbids the traffic-light pattern
findings.summary: All disclosure label categories render in one uniform colour to signal neutrality, not a scale and explicitly not green/red. A scale would imply a value judgement about whether AI involvement was good or bad. Use colour scales for risk (scalar); uniform colour for provenance categories (categorical).

findings.title: Disclosure has a budget
findings.summary: C2PA examined an 'AI-enhanced' label and rejected it: the enhancement is frequent and expected, so the label would surface constantly, become redundant, and lose meaning. Every warning spends from a finite attention budget.

findings.title: The waterline is where trust UX fails
findings.summary: Governance facts (is this verifier registered, for what purpose, under whose authority) are the hardest to render and the most consequential to omit. Products render the Agency and Engineering tips well and leave the straddling Governance layer invisible.

findings.title: The market's weakest moments are T4, T5, T8
findings.summary: Counterparty identification, request comprehension, and retrospection are the least-solved across shipping products. T3 (custody) is best-studied and still unsolved; T9 (repair) is almost entirely unaddressed outside a few crypto wallets.

findings.title: The biggest unexploited transfer: simulation to identity
findings.summary: The crypto-wallet 'here is what will be true afterward' reframing is the strongest calibration device in the corpus and has never been evaluated for identity attribute disclosure. The most promising single experiment.

findings.title: Design for calibrated reliance, not maximal trust
findings.summary: A trust moment is a decision under uncertainty, and the goal is confidence that matches real reliability. Over-trust (misuse) and under-trust (disuse) are both failures. Every moment carries a default posture, Increase / Hold / Decrease / Suspend, and every increase in authority, disclosure or irreversibility must be matched by an increase in evidence, clarity or control.

findings.title: AI-content labels are brittle and can over-fire
findings.summary: Canada's transparency consultation notes text watermarks remain easy to remove, so durable provenance (C2PA-style metadata) has to back any visible cue. Labelling frequent, expected AI edits produces banner blindness, the same finite-attention problem the disclosure-budget finding describes.

antipatterns.name: The unattributed badge
antipatterns.desc: A 'Verified' mark with no path to who verified, against what criteria, when
antipatterns.where: Marketplaces, profile systems, AI vendor listings

antipatterns.name: Binary trust
antipatterns.desc: Two states only, so absence of warning reads as safety

antipatterns.name: Consent theatre
antipatterns.desc: A single unbundled all-or-nothing choice, styled as control
antipatterns.where: mDL and eID pilots; app permission flows

antipatterns.name: Hash as description
antipatterns.desc: Presenting a digest, address, or DID as if it conveyed meaning

antipatterns.name: Warning inflation
antipatterns.desc: Alerting on everything, so users learn to dismiss reflexively

antipatterns.name: Confidence laundering
antipatterns.desc: Rendering a low-confidence output with high-confidence styling

antipatterns.name: Asymmetric revocation
antipatterns.desc: One tap to grant, six screens to withdraw

antipatterns.name: Skeuomorphic overreach
antipatterns.desc: Institutional security language on a self-asserted claim

antipatterns.name: Amnesia by design
antipatterns.desc: No record of what was shared with whom

antipatterns.name: The dead-end warning
antipatterns.desc: Risk flagged, no path to dispute, abandon, or understand

antipatterns.name: Sovereignty without affordances
antipatterns.desc: Control claimed in marketing, not matched by disclosure, revocation, or portability

antipatterns.name: Novelty opacity
antipatterns.desc: Failing to explain what the new thing is; users default to old mental models

open_questions.q: Does the disclosure receipt change behaviour?
open_questions.detail: No published study tests whether a durable, reviewable log of one's own disclosures changes subsequent disclosure decisions. Testable, cheap, a strong contribution.
eIDAS 2.0 makes registered scope machine-checkable. Nobody has tested whether surfacing a scope mismatch at the consent moment changes behaviour, or just produces another habituated warning.

open_questions.q: Does transaction simulation transfer to identity disclosure?
open_questions.detail: The strongest calibration device in the corpus, never evaluated for identity attribute disclosure. The most promising single experiment identified.

open_questions.q: The implied truth effect in provenance labelling
open_questions.detail: C2PA flags it in the spec as an open user-research question. Unresolved and directly relevant to AI content-disclosure regimes now in force.
How fast should autonomy expand, on what evidence, and what must the demotion affordance look like? Almost no empirical work exists; the deployment wave is arriving now.
